Agentic AI for Utility Operators.title: Agentic AI for Utility Operators
points: Real power-sector uses, engineering tools and measured research results
One teaching session with two worked exercises
IEEE ComSoc theme / Evidence reviewed 17 October 2026
Agentic AI for Utility Operators.note: All slides belong to the main presentation. The opening distinguishes systems in use, utility statements and product announcements. Every agent-research paper covers a power-system task. We explain LangGraph and task dependency graphs through fault analysis and weather-risk studies. A separate follow-on workshop covers the detailed GridGuard cases on voltage, restoration and cyber events.

What is agentic AI?.title: What is agentic AI?
points: Here, agentic AI means a system that uses feedback to choose and adjust actions toward a goal.
The system combines a decision model, saved progress (state), callable tools and rules for carrying out actions.
This is our working definition. Researchers use “agent” and “agentic system” in several ways.
What is agentic AI?.note: The first sentence is our summary, not a quotation or a standard definition. Anthropic includes both programmed workflows and LLM-directed agents under agentic systems. Wooldridge and Jennings also discuss different definitions of an agent. The later examples focus on engineering systems using large language models, or LLMs. “Agentic” describes how the whole system pursues a task. It is not another software component beside the agent. A system can use just one agent.
What is agentic AI?.eyebrow: A working definition based on the literature

What is an AI agent?.title: What is an AI agent?
points: Russell and Norvig describe an agent as something that observes its environment and acts on it.
An agent can use rules, planning, optimization or learning. A large language model (LLM) is one possible way to choose actions.
What is an AI agent?.note: The equation is teaching notation: the policy uses the history of observations to choose the next action. It is not the textbook’s exact notation. The agent function is this abstract mapping, and a program implements it. A grid-study agent may observe case files and solver logs, then call a tool, ask for information or return a report. This classical definition predates LLMs. It also includes many older forms of automation. The linked sample chapter is from the second edition, even though its URL says fourth edition. The reading guide records that difference.

An agent chooses actions; a tool exposes.title: An agent chooses a step. A tool runs it.
points: The agent reads the evidence and chooses an allowed action. The tool carries out the request through a defined software interface.
A tool can give access to a solver, database or another agent. The solver computes the electrical result.
An agent chooses actions; a tool exposes.caption: Teaching example: diagnose a fixed study case without changing it. The tool interface calls the solver.
An agent chooses actions; a tool exposes.note: A run_pf request should identify the study case. Its response should include status, numerical results and an evidence ID. The solver computes the electrical result. After an error, an LLM may choose another allowed check or stop and ask for help. The runtime software saves progress and carries out those choices. This example gives no permission to switch live equipment. A service may contain its own agents and still act as a tool for the agent calling it.

Workflow and agent: who directs the next.title: Workflow or agent: who chooses the next step?
points: Anthropic calls a process a workflow when code sets its paths. An agent lets the LLM choose some steps and tools.
Code can also route tasks, run parallel workers or repeat repairs. A loop alone does not make a process an agent.
excerpt: Fixed steps: load case, run power flow, check, report
LLM choice: choose a check after observing an error
Both need limits and a clear stopping rule
Workflow and agent: who directs the next.note: This distinction comes from Anthropic’s practitioner account. It is useful engineering language, not a universal definition. Its workflow patterns include routing, orchestrator-workers and evaluator-optimizer loops. A system can combine fixed requirements with an LLM choosing among allowed next steps. PowerDAG later shows this combination.

Agency is relative to a goal and an oper.title: An agent needs a clear goal and limits
points: Wooldridge and Jennings describe agents that act with some independence, respond to change, pursue goals and interact with others.
A study assistant may choose diagnostic checks while the operator keeps authority over operational actions.
Define the available evidence, allowed actions, work budget and conditions for success or asking for help.
Agency is relative to a goal and an oper.note: These points paraphrase the authors’ historical “weak notion of agency.” Independence is relative to the task. It does not imply unrestricted control of physical equipment. Judge an action using the evidence and performance goal available at the time. A rational choice does not guarantee success. For a fixed v43 study case, a complete report explaining what remains unresolved may satisfy an advisory task when the allowed checks cannot solve it.

Framework, platform and application iden.title: Frameworks, platforms and applications do different jobs
points: LangGraph is software that manages saved state, routing, persistence across pauses and workflow execution.
Harvard’s PowerAgent is a power-system community and platform. PowerDAG is a specific research system.
A numerical solver calculates how the electrical model behaves.
Framework, platform and application iden.note: These names refer to different roles. LangGraph can run both fixed workflows and processes where a model chooses steps. PowerAgent develops power-system models, tool interfaces and workflows. Later slides show a specific LangGraph example in its PowerWF repository. PowerDAG has its own supervisory design. A platform name alone does not establish numerical accuracy or deployment at a utility.

The engineering question behind the news.title: Which parts of the job can an agent do?
points: Which parts of a power-system task can an agent coordinate? Which results must come from a trusted engineering tool?
We will examine reported deployments and research workflows, then define checks an operator can use to accept a result.
The engineering question behind the news.note: We study the whole engineering workflow. A named deployment, a product announcement, a research demonstration and a controlled test provide different kinds of evidence. The cases cover input preparation, outage analysis and planning support. We then examine how agents coordinate numerical tools.

April–June 2026: HyperQ enters PJM’s app.title: PJM uses HyperQ to review connection applications
points: Tapestry’s June 2026 report says HyperQ entered PJM Cycle 1 on 29 April. PJM confirmed testing in March.
Gemini agents check site-control agreements (rights to use land), property parcels and tariff evidence. Engineers make final decisions.
This work checks application readiness before the electrical study begins.
April–June 2026: HyperQ enters PJM’s app.note: Tapestry’s 11 June report covers 811 generation applications. Agents perform limited document and evidence tasks. The report does not establish an agent making a power-flow conclusion or an automatic regulatory decision. The system guides the agents’ work and records evidence citations. The article describes migration to Google ADK as future work, so do not label the deployed system an established ADK implementation.
April–June 2026: HyperQ enters PJM’s app.takeaway: A numerical study needs reliable input evidence.
April–June 2026: HyperQ enters PJM’s app.eyebrow: United States / Supplier reports deployment / PJM confirms earlier testing

HyperQ: the reported computational workl.title: HyperQ: what the reported numbers measure
points: The timings cover computer processing for 811 applications. They exclude document-transfer time and human validation.
HyperQ: the reported computational workl.caption: Original Tapestry performance graphic, June 2026. The timing covers only computer processing.
HyperQ: the reported computational workl.note: The supplier reports grouping 4,581 raw site-control documents into 2,328 bundles and checking four criteria. The graphic’s 9,312 macro-assessments are not 9,312 projects. The full interconnection process also includes document transfer and human review. The report gives no confusion matrix or accuracy denominator. We omit its historical 20x headline because it compares manual work with computer processing using different work and timing boundaries.

2026 CAISO/OATI report: agents in daily.title: CAISO/OATI: agents help review planned outages
points: OATI’s AI Genie uses Workflow, Advisor and Recon agents under one coordinator. Operators keep final authority.
The supplier reports processing 500+ next-day requests nightly in under eight minutes. It gives no per-request time or reviewer-effort result.
2026 CAISO/OATI report: agents in daily.caption: Real California ISO control room. OATI supplies the batch result and later production-use claim.
2026 CAISO/OATI report: agents in daily.note: California ISO’s July 2025 account described a pilot. OATI’s 2026 field report describes daily production use but gives no exact production start date. The reported inequalities imply more than 62.5 requests per minute for the batch. They do not describe individual request latency. Do not compare eight machine-minutes with a separate analyst-hours figure as though both came from the same trial. The work prepares outage analysis and operating evidence. Reviewers make final decisions.
2026 CAISO/OATI report: agents in daily.takeaway: A processing rate needs a clear work boundary and a measure of the review left for people.

September 2026: Duke and AWS coordinate.title: Duke and AWS: agents help prepare planning studies
points: Duke engineers use AWS-managed agents to prepare study cases and coordinate interconnection studies for new grid connections.
A September 2026 AWS announcement reports data preparation falling from two weeks of manual work to hours.
The final number of hours is unspecified. Engineers keep final responsibility for engineering decisions.
September 2026: Duke and AWS coordinate.caption: Duke operator, 2022, shown for context. The reported agents support planning, rather than this pictured operating desk.
September 2026: Duke and AWS coordinate.note: AWS’s 17 September 2026 announcement names Duke engineers using agents to coordinate studies. The agents prepare inputs and coordinate existing physics software, models and scripts. The report says data preparation fell from two weeks of manual work to hours. It gives neither the final number of hours nor a sample count. It identifies no SDK, model or runtime. Do not infer Strands or AgentCore from the cloud provider. Engineers make final decisions.
September 2026: Duke and AWS coordinate.takeaway: Faster preparation alone does not establish a shorter full regulatory process.

May 2026: agentic PSS E capabilities are.title: Siemens announces agents for PSS E planning studies
points: Siemens’ Gridscale X announcement describes agents coordinating transmission-planning simulations.
The targets include connection studies for large loads and data centers, using open software interfaces (APIs).
The announcement does not name a production user of the new agentic PSS E features.
May 2026: agentic PSS E capabilities are.note: The same release describes Alliander’s migration to the platform. That shows platform adoption, not use of the newly announced agentic PSS E features. The claim of up to 50% faster study response has no disclosed benchmark method, so we do not plot it. The announcement shows a possible integration path: agents coordinate an established simulation environment.
May 2026: agentic PSS E capabilities are.takeaway: Check product features and measured utility results separately.

May 2026: National Grid reports agentic.title: National Grid reports agents checking project plans
points: The results transcript says its “capital control tower” already checks early project options and documents at approval stages.
Project managers get feedback while they can still change their plans.
The group reports no agent framework, timing result or accuracy result.
May 2026: National Grid reports agentic.note: The CEO’s 14 May 2026 results transcript reports agentic project-assurance use. “Capital control tower” names the system supporting project checks. Later comments about optimizing access outages describe future plans. Do not attribute nearby FLISR, outage-minute or gas-crew results to this agent. The source verifies reported use without supporting a numerical performance estimate.
May 2026: National Grid reports agentic.eyebrow: Reported current use / UK–US group / Rollout location unspecified

NYPA: agentic AI discussion and the data.title: NYPA: better data for agent use
points: In an October 2026 webinar, NYPA’s data-quality lead describes Databricks and Ataccama checks that meter data must pass.
A separate demo shows Genie asking Ataccama, through MCP, whether data can be trusted.
NYPA discusses meter-data pipelines. The agent demo uses a product/reorder table, so it does not show a NYPA grid-control agent.
NYPA: agentic AI discussion and the data.note: This supplier-hosted webinar discusses NYPA’s quality checks for frequently arriving meter data. The separate demo uses Genie and an Ataccama MCP service with a product/reorder table. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is a standard way to connect AI systems to tools and data. Keep the NYPA implementation and the generic agent demo separate. We use October 2026 because the fetched event and on-demand report show adjacent dates. These sources support the discussion of data agents need, without establishing a production grid-command agent at NYPA. We excluded the earlier governance-agenda search result because the full original was unavailable.
NYPA: agentic AI discussion and the data.eyebrow: New York Power Authority / Named speaker discussing implementation

Eversource: an engineering path toward a.title: Eversource: adding agentic skills to grid studies
points: Eversource already uses MATLAB with Synergi Electric to study a range of possible conditions on distribution networks.
An October 2026 engineering job posting asks for agentic and AI-based workflows in MATLAB.
This shows the skills Eversource wants to add. A job posting does not prove deployment of an agent platform.
Eversource: an engineering path toward a.note: The April 2025 MathWorks report describes probabilistic distribution studies. These use Monte Carlo sampling and parallel numerical simulations to examine many possible conditions. Its timing improvement belongs to conventional simulation automation, so we do not show it as an agent result. Eversource’s October 2026 posting concerns distribution-system modeling and automation and explicitly mentions agentic MATLAB workflows. It shows the company seeking this capability for an existing simulation environment.
Eversource: an engineering path toward a.eyebrow: Eversource / Existing simulation tools and a stated engineering direction

GE Vernova: the grid platform supporting.title: GE Vernova: a platform that can connect grid tools
points: Alabama Power’s use of GridOS for Distribution gives a named example of GE Vernova’s grid platform.
GridOS provides shared software for coordinating grid work. This shows where study tools and operator workflows could connect.
The public statement does not separate out a reliability improvement caused by agents.
GE Vernova: the grid platform supporting.caption: Official GridOS promotional composite. The platform example does not establish a measured agent-specific result.
GE Vernova: the grid platform supporting.note: This GE example concerns GE Vernova’s electric-power business. The February 2026 GridOS announcement names a utility context. It does not establish a specific autonomous LLM controller. Our teaching example explains what an integrated agent would also need: clear tool interfaces, saved state, evidence checks and limits on its authority.
GE Vernova: the grid platform supporting.takeaway: For each case, identify the customer, task, agent’s role and measured result.

Operator attention is a scarce resource.title: Operators often work against a deadline
points: A PNNL survey of 20 control-room operators reported that, on average, 61% of tasks needed completion in under 30 minutes.
The survey had 75 questions. It gives no task count or statistical spread behind that average.
An assistant should reduce the time people spend finding and reviewing evidence within the task’s deadline.
Operator attention is a scarce resource.caption: Duke Energy control room, 2022. The PNNL survey is a separate study.
Operator attention is a scarce resource.note: The 61% is an average share of tasks performed or supported. It is not the percentage of operators. The source gives neither the task denominator nor variance. Twenty respondents do not support a binomial interval for that 61%. Seventy-five survey items do not imply 1,500 independent timing observations. This small self-report study is not a national estimate. Ask which tasks need quick decisions and which allow more investigation.
Operator attention is a scarce resource.takeaway: Measure the operator’s total effort and deadline alongside AI response time.

Three questions behind a usable recommen.title: Three checks for a useful recommendation
points: Data: do the asset, units, time and grid connections (topology) match the question?
Engineering: does the solution meet the requested equations and limits?
Decision: is there enough evidence for the next step the user is allowed to take?
Three questions behind a usable recommen.note: These are separate checks. A correctly formatted call may still use old grid connections. An optimization may converge after changing a variable the user was not allowed to change. A correct result may still leave part of the decision unanswered. These checks form the acceptance contract: the agreed conditions a result must meet. We reuse it in the examples and exercises.
Three questions behind a usable recommen.takeaway: Agree on acceptance checks for the whole task.

Define the task before selecting the mod.title: A clear task makes success easier to test
points: The task is to check whether an earlier study result still applies after a new event.
Return evidence or ask for missing data. Stop if inputs change, a tool fails, the work budget runs out or permission is missing.
excerpt: case = F12 / event at 15:02 / review at 15:05
snapshot = {data_time, topology_hash, model_revision}
allowed_output = recommendation or request_for_evidence
Define the task before selecting the mod.note: All F12 records and policies are invented teaching data, not utility operating rules. A snapshot identifies the data time, grid-connection version and model revision. Start by identifying the user, the result they need and the actions they may take. Success means meeting these agreed requirements. Answer length and the number of tool calls do not establish success.
Define the task before selecting the mod.takeaway: A clear task gives us a clear way to check success.

An agent chooses calls; tools produce ob.title: Agents choose requests. Tools return results.
points: a is the tool request, h is the recorded interaction history, and nu identifies the saved input snapshot.
The software checks each request, runs it and adds the returned evidence to the history.
An agent chooses calls; tools produce ob.note: The equation describes a software interface. It does not assume we observe the full physical system or that the history has the Markov property, meaning it contains everything needed to predict the next state. The model chooses a request using the goal and previous evidence. The software runs a service against a specific input snapshot. A historian, which stores time-stamped measurements, returns measured data. A simulator returns model results. Selecting either tool does not turn its output into a command to physical equipment.
An agent chooses calls; tools produce ob.takeaway: Check the tool requests, their inputs and their results.

A useful trace includes the branch that.title: When data are stale, the next step is to stop
points: The asset lookup succeeds, but the measurement request marks the data as stale, meaning out of date.
Ask for current evidence. The original task remains unresolved.
A useful trace includes the branch that.caption: Invented trace showing tool inputs, returned results and a decision to stop.
A useful trace includes the branch that.note: A trace records the sequence of tool requests and results. Walk through the IDs and times in the drawing. When required data are unavailable or out of date, the system should say so. It must not invent a value or silently reuse an older one. Check whether the agent detects the problem and asks for the right update. A trace makes this inspection possible but does not itself prove the work is correct.

A typed contract prevents a concrete uni.title: Unit checks catch a kV versus p.u. mistake
points: 12.47 kV is 1.00 per unit (p.u.) only with a 12.47 kV base. Per unit means value divided by base.
A tool expecting p.u. must reject a raw kV value or require explicit information for converting it.
A typed contract prevents a concrete uni.caption: Teaching example with invented values. These values are not recommended operating limits.
A typed contract prevents a concrete uni.note: The software interface must enforce units. Prompt wording alone is insufficient. The same number can mean very different physical quantities. Check unit labels, the chosen base and the asset ID in software. A valid type or unit still does not prove that the measurement or model is accurate. The diagram shows both the error and the information needed to fix it.

A new topology invalidates the old resul.title: A study must match the current grid connections
points: The old study used a closed switch and grid version v42. The event opens the switch and creates version v43.
Update the inputs and repeat the affected calculations. Rewriting the explanation does not update the numerical result.
A new topology invalidates the old resul.caption: Invented before-and-after network. This illustration does not calculate power flow.
A new topology invalidates the old resul.note: Point to the switch that changed. The old result represents different grid connections, rather than simply an older timestamp. Version matching is a necessary consistency check. It still leaves two questions: does the model represent the real grid accurately, and do the refreshed measurements represent the event?

Convergence is conditional engineering e.title: A solver result depends on the problem it solves
points: u is the proposed decision, x is the modeled state, and m and tau identify the model and grid connections.
A feasible solution meets the stated equations and limits. You still need to check study coverage and permission to act.
Convergence is conditional engineering e.note: Keep solver status, equation errors (residuals) and modeled limit checks separate from whether the analysis covers the full request. A solver can converge on the wrong problem. The study requirements must state constraints and tolerances, meaning the allowed numerical error. This slide sets no universal voltage or loading limit. Permission to act remains a separate software and organizational decision.
Convergence is conditional engineering e.takeaway: Report the problem and assumptions together with the solver result.

Exercise 1: audit three returned packets.title: Exercise 1: check three returned data packets
points: For this exercise, data must be at most 60 s old, use topology v43 and use p.u. The user can recommend actions only.
Which packet passes? Explain why each other packet fails.
Does passing these checks establish complete engineering validity or permission to execute an action?
excerpt: A = {age_s:20, topology:v42, unit:pu}
B = {age_s:15, topology:v43, unit:kV}
C = {age_s:45, topology:v43, unit:pu}
Exercise 1: audit three returned packets.note: Allow 1 minute to inspect, 2 minutes in pairs, 2 minutes to share and 1 minute to debrief. age_s means age in seconds. Only C passes the stated initial checks. A has the wrong grid version. B has the wrong unit. C still needs the right asset mapping, a valid model, the required engineering checks, enough scenario coverage and an explanation people can review. The user may advise but cannot execute actions. The 60-second rule is made up for this exercise. It is not a general operating standard.

Power-system research asks different eng.title: Power-system papers test different tasks
points: Fault-analysis tools find events in recorded waveforms. Simulation assistants set up and run studies.
Control prototypes suggest actions in model grids. Benchmarks test how well systems find evidence or answer numerical questions.
Each result applies to the tested task, tools, allowed actions and test cases.
Power-system research asks different eng.note: Every paper that follows concerns power systems. They measure different outcomes, so their percentages cannot form a ranking across papers. The numerical solver computes the engineering result. The language model selects tools and helps interpret the returned evidence.

Harvard PowerAgent: a roadmap and domain.title: Harvard PowerAgent: models, tools and study workflows
points: Zhang and Xie’s 2025 IEEE roadmap combines AI models, software tools and study workflows.
PowerFM targets power-system modeling. PowerMCP connects tools. PowerWF provides study workflows.
PowerAgent is the wider initiative. PowerAgentBench-Dyn later tests specific dynamic-study tasks, which examine grid behavior over time.
Harvard PowerAgent: a roadmap and domain.note: Full citation: Qian Zhang and Le Xie, PowerAgent: A Road Map Toward Agentic Intelligence in Power Systems: Foundation Model, Model Context Protocol, and Workflow, IEEE Power and Energy Magazine 23(5), 93–101, September–October 2025, DOI 10.1109/MPE.2025.3579718. A foundation model is a pretrained model intended for reuse across tasks. We verified the architecture through the authors’ full ERCOT presentation and official project page. The publisher/preprint download was unavailable, so we attribute no uninspected experimental results to the article. The community and repositories keep changing. Their current features are not a fixed 2025 benchmark.

PowerAgent example: study the impact of.title: PowerAgent example: what changes when load is added?
points: PowerWF’s Grid Impact Evaluation uses LangGraph to coordinate studies in PowerWorld.
It runs power flow and outage checks before and after adding load, then summarizes the changes.
excerpt: Inputs: PowerWorld case + bus + added MW
Before added load: power flow and outage checks
After added load: power flow and outage checks
Compare the original and changed study results
PowerAgent example: study the impact of.note: This is a specific current workflow maintained by the authors. It does not establish one SDK for the whole PowerAgent initiative. In the code, graph.py imports StateGraph and ToolNode, saves workflow flags and returns from the shared tools node to the relevant step. A bus is a connection point in the model. The author presentation discusses load-growth and data-center studies using power flow, congestion, voltage and N−1 checks, which examine single-component outages. The code and demonstrations show the workflow. They provide no controlled utility timing or reliability estimate. The reading guide links the exact source file.

DrAgent: a recorded fault becomes a sequ.title: DrAgent: reading a recorded grid fault
points: The third current trace shows the fault. Dashed lines mark its start, highest current and clearance (when the fault ends).
DrAgent: a recorded fault becomes a sequ.caption: Original DrAgent Figure 2, PDF p.4. The third current channel shows a fault in a sample disturbance record.
DrAgent: a recorded fault becomes a sequ.note: The Hitachi Energy paper studies disturbance analysis on transmission lines. This is an original figure extracted from the research paper, not an invented event or a live operating screen. First identify how the curve changes. Numerical tools return a sample index or current measurement. The task still requires an engineering interpretation of those values.

DrAgent: a plan connects domain-specific.title: DrAgent: one tool provides input for the next
points: DrAgent plans first, then uses LangChain/LangGraph and Python tools on COMTRADE disturbance files. The paper calls this a ReWOO-style plan.
One tool’s result can become the next tool’s input. Check both the input format and its engineering meaning.
excerpt: Teaching example of a tool dependency:
inception_sample = find_fault_inception(record)
inception_seconds = inception_sample / sampling_rate
The report combines timing and current measurements
DrAgent: a plan connects domain-specific.note: ReWOO plans the work before running tools that use earlier results. COMTRADE is a format for recorded power-system disturbances. The implementation uses Gemini 1.5Pro for planning, a dozen domain functions and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over 138 product manuals. RAG retrieves relevant source text for the model. The excerpt is simplified teaching notation. To convert a fault’s starting sample to seconds, the system first needs both the sample index and sampling rate. This dependency motivates the next graph explanation.

DrAgent result: numerical tools help, bu.title: DrAgent: more correct answers, with errors still present
points: We counted scores of 2 or more as correct across the paper’s 18 recorded cases.
Timing the fault’s end remains harder. The grading rules also accept a correctly labeled fault duration.
DrAgent result: numerical tools help, bu.caption: Counts reconstructed from Table IV and the Appendix. They are neither new experiments nor the paper’s mean-score measure.
DrAgent result: numerical tools help, bu.note: Fault inception: baseline 12/18, agent 18/18. Maximum current: baseline 16/18, agent 18/18. Clearance/timing: baseline 4/18, agent 13/18. The paper allows 3 ms timing error and 5% current error. One expert graded the answers. Q6 footnote 8 accepts a correctly labeled duration, so these are not strictly clearance-timestamp accuracy counts. The printed Q6 mean conflicts with the individual cells. This chart therefore uses the audited cell counts.

Three graphs describe different parts of.title: Three kinds of graph have different jobs
points: An electrical network graph shows buses (connection points) and electrical equipment.
A task dependency graph shows which calculation needs which earlier result.
A LangGraph execution graph shows workflow steps and rules for choosing the next step.
Three graphs describe different parts of.note: A radial feeder has a tree-like electrical layout, but its software can still contain loops. A calculation graph without loops can analyze a meshed electrical network. State which graph you mean before discussing a node, connection or loop. A software architecture drawing is not the electrical model.

A DAG exposes the prerequisites of a cal.title: A DAG shows which result must come first
points: DAG means directed acyclic graph: arrows show dependencies, and no path loops back to its start.
Independent calculations can run together once their inputs exist. Combine their outputs after every required result arrives.
A DAG exposes the prerequisites of a cal.caption: Original teaching adaptation of DrAgent’s tool dependencies, rather than its exact execution graph.
A DAG exposes the prerequisites of a cal.note: Every task must follow the tasks that produce its inputs. This is a valid topological order. Fault-start sample and sampling rate must both exist before the time conversion runs. Finding maximum current can run independently of that conversion when both use the same unchanged record. Dependencies determine which tasks can run together. The positions of boxes in a drawing do not.

LangGraph supports state and conditional.title: LangGraph can repeat steps when a check fails
points: Each node (workflow step) reads saved state and returns an update. A routing rule can send the run back to an earlier step.
Set a retry limit. End with success or a clear unresolved result.
LangGraph supports state and conditional.caption: Teaching example with two allowed retries. It illustrates routing rather than a paper’s exact code.
LangGraph supports state and conditional.note: LangGraph is software for running workflows. It can support loops, unlike a DAG. StateGraph defines stored state fields and workflow nodes. Application-defined reducers specify how updates from parallel steps combine. A node may call an engineering tool with fixed rules or an AI model. The application must define validation, stopping and permissions. Running the graph does not prove that an electrical solution is feasible.

State must identify the study being resu.title: Saved state must identify the study and its evidence
points: Save the case ID, input versions, evidence, status and attempt count.
Label each result with its case or outage ID. This helps reveal missing or duplicate results when parallel work comes together.
excerpt: case_id = C17; topology = v43; model = m7
evidence = {outage_6:R1, outage_7:R2}
expected = {outage_6, outage_7, outage_34}
status = INCOMPLETE; attempts = 1
State must identify the study being resu.note: These invented state fields illustrate a software contract. They are not a built-in LangGraph schema for power systems. Here, the expected set includes outage_34 but the evidence does not. Default update behavior does not guarantee that all branch results survive a merge. Define and test the reducer, or an external evidence store, to preserve case IDs and detect duplicates or missing outputs.
State must identify the study being resu.takeaway: Saved state identifies the evidence. The application still has to check it.

A checkpoint preserves state across a pa.title: A checkpoint lets a workflow pause and resume
points: A checkpoint saves progress. A thread_id identifies the same workflow history when the run resumes.
If grid connections change during the pause, the software must reject or recompute affected old results before using them.
A checkpoint preserves state across a pa.caption: Teaching example: saved progress may contain results for an older grid version.
A checkpoint preserves state across a pa.note: An interrupt can pause for outside review and later resume in the same thread. Current LangGraph documentation says the interrupted node restarts from its beginning. Actions before the interrupt can therefore happen again. Use stable step IDs or other idempotency controls, which prevent repeated execution from applying the same change twice. This example grants no permission to command live grid equipment.

Parallel contingency studies need an exp.title: Parallel outage studies must account for every case
points: Run each selected outage on a separate, consistent copy of the same starting grid case.
Before combining results, compare the returned case IDs with the expected list. Mark failed or missing cases as unresolved.
Parallel contingency studies need an exp.caption: Invented example with three outage cases. It contains no calculated numerical results.
Parallel contingency studies need an exp.note: The goal is complete evidence for the selected study scope, rather than a count of completed software steps. If C2 fails, the output should name C2, explain its failure and state what remains unknown. This applies AgentiGrid’s lesson about incomplete coverage. Completing a selected set of outages does not prove coverage of every N−1 contingency, meaning every relevant single-component outage.

PowerDAG: supervise a distribution-grid.title: PowerDAG checks the steps needed before a tool runs
points: PowerDAG finds relevant verified workflow examples. It uses a dependency graph and a gate that checks required earlier tool calls.
The benchmark covers 108 tools, ten task families and four Vermont feeder models (local distribution networks).
excerpt: Find relevant verified workflow examples
Propose a tool call with the current inputs
Check that required Write tools have already run
